sentences: White birch trunks stand close together across the whole canvas.
A few have been cut down, opening a gap, and beyond it two little girls are picking berries.
This is Foxgloves, painted by the Norwegian artist Nikolai Astrup.
It is painted in oil on canvas, 77 centimetres high and 99 centimetres wide, around 1919 or 1920.
It belongs to the Norwegian foundation Sparebankstiftelsen DNB and can be seen at KODE, the art museums of Bergen.
Look first at the birches.
Their white trunks stand close together right across the picture.
Like a screen drawn across the woods, they make our eyes pause before going further in.
Now look through the opening.
Two girls are picking berries.
As the foundation's description notes, they are placed symmetrically, and together with the trunks they give the whole picture a calm, serene mood.
Find the little stream winding down the slope, its water running briskly.
In this still wood, the only things moving are the stream and the girls' busy hands.
Now look at the foreground.
Among the moss-covered stones and birch trunks, tall spikes of foxglove rise up.
The flower gives the painting its title.
In English it is called the foxglove.
The landscape is Jølster, Astrup's home valley.
Born in 1880, he moved there at the age of three, when his father became the parish priest.
As the eldest son he was expected to join the priesthood, but at about seventeen he left his studies to become an artist.
He trained at Harriet Backer's painting school in Kristiania, now Oslo, and studied in Paris in 1901 and 1902.
But by the spring of 1902 he was back in Jølster.
He is said to have claimed later that it was in Paris that he realised what Jølster could become in paint.
Astrup was a painter, a printmaker and a gardener who worked his own land.
He married Engel in 1907 and they had eight children, but he suffered from asthma and lung disease all his life and died of pneumonia in January 1928.
The foundation describes him as one of Norway's most beloved artists, a painter who helped shape the way Norwegians see and understand their own landscape.
Step back and see it whole: the rhythm of white trunks, the small figures between them, the flowers at our feet.
Today, take a slow look at a familiar view near your home that you usually walk straight past.
